title: Subsequence With the Minimum Score
statement: You are given two strings `s` and `t`. You may delete any set of characters from `t` (possibly none, possibly all) so that what remains of `t` is a subsequence of `s`: its characters appear in `s` in the same relative order, not necessarily next to each other. The *score* of a deletion is `0` when nothing is deleted; otherwise it is `right - left + 1`, where `left` and `right` are the smallest and largest original indices (0-indexed) in `t` of the deleted characters. Return the smallest score that makes `t` a subsequence of `s`. Deleting every character always works, since the empty string is a subsequence of any string.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The score only depends on the first and last deleted positions, so once you delete `t[left]` and `t[right - 1]` you may as well delete everything between them for free: it never raises the score and only makes matching easier. So the real question is which contiguous block `t[left..right-1]` to delete so that the prefix `t[0..left-1]` followed by the suffix `t[right..]` is a subsequence of `s`. Trying every block and testing it is O(m² · n); greedy matching from both ends plus two pointers does it in linear time.

## Approach

1. Match `t` from the back against `s` from the back, as late as possible. `suffix[j]` is the latest index of `s` where `t[j..]` can start, or `-1` when `t[j..]` is not a subsequence. Set `suffix[m] = n` for the empty suffix.
2. Let `right` be the first `j` with `suffix[j] >= 0`. Deleting `t[0..right-1]` works, so `best = right`.
3. Scan `s` with index `i`, matching `t` from the front as early as possible; `left` counts the matched prefix.
4. Each time `t[left]` matches `s[i]`, increase `left`, then push `right` forward until `right >= left` and the suffix starts after `i` (`suffix[right] > i`). Both conditions only get stricter, so `right` never moves back.
5. The block `t[left..right-1]` is then deletable; update `best` with `right - left`. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abacaba"`, `t = "bzaa"`. From the back, `t[3] = 'a'` matches `s[6]`, `t[2] = 'a'` matches `s[4]`, and `'z'` never matches, so `suffix = [-1, -1, 4, 6, 7]`. The first valid suffix is `right = 2`, giving `best = 2`. Scanning `s`, `t[0] = 'b'` matches at `i = 1`, so `left = 1`; `suffix[2] = 4 > 1` keeps `right = 2`, and `best = 2 - 1 = 1`. `'z'` never matches again, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): each of `pos`, `i` and `right` only moves one way.
- Space: O(m) for `suffix`.

## Pitfalls

- Matching the prefix early and the suffix late is what makes the test `suffix[right] > i` exact; matching them any other way can reject a valid split.
- `right` must also stay at least `left`, or the kept prefix and suffix would overlap in `t`.
- When `t` is already a subsequence the answer is `0`, not `1`; `suffix[0] >= 0` gives `best = 0` at once.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n`, `m` | lengths of `s` and `t` |
| `suffix` | `suffix[j]` = latest start in `s` for `t[j..]`, `-1` if impossible |
| `pos` | pointer into `s` while matching from the back |
| `i`, `left` | pointer into `s` and length of the matched prefix of `t` |
| `right` | start of the kept suffix of `t` |
| `best` | smallest score found so far |
